vsm1.1:25.1: 25. (v) Now, here is the answer to the question, HOW MANY KINDS OF VIRTUE ARE THERE?
vsm1.1:25.2: 1. Firstly all this virtue is of one kind by reason of its own characteristic of composing.
vsm1.1:25.3: 2. It is of two kinds as keeping and avoiding.
vsm1.1:25.4: 3. Likewise as that of good behaviour and that of the beginning of the life of purity, 4. As abstinence and non-abstinence,
vsm1.1:25.5: 5. As dependent and independent, 6. As temporary and lifelong,
vsm1.1:25.6: 7. As limited and unlimited, 8. As mundane and supramundane.
vsm1.1:25.7: 9. It is of three kinds as inferior, medium, and superior.
vsm1.1:25.8:
10. Likewise as giving precedence to self, giving precedence to the world, and giving
precedence to the Dhamma, 11. As adhered to, not adhered to, and tranquillized.
vsm1.1:25.9:
12. As purified, unpurified, and dubious. 13. As that of the trainer,
that of the non-trainer, and that of the neither-trainer-nor-non-trainer.
vsm1.1:25.10: 14. It is of four kinds as partaking of diminution, of stagnation, of distinction, of penetration.
vsm1.1:25.11:
15. Likewise as that of bhikkhus, of bhikkhunīs, of the not-fully-admitted, of the laity, 16.
As natural, customary, necessary, due to previous causes,
vsm1.1:25.12:
17. As virtue of Pātimokkha restraint, of restraint of sense
faculties, of purification of livelihood, and that concerning requisites.
vsm1.1:25.13: 18. It is of five kinds as virtue consisting in limited purification, etc.;
vsm1.1:25.14:
for this is said in the Paṭisambhidā: “Five kinds of virtue: virtue consisting in limited
purification, virtue consisting in unlimited purification,
vsm1.1:25.15: virtue consisting in fulfilled purification, virtue consisting in unadhered-to purification,
vsm1.1:25.16: virtue consisting in tranquillized purification” (Paṭis I 42).
vsm1.1:25.17: 19. Likewise as abandoning, refraining, volition, restraint, and non-transgression.
vsm1.1:26.1: 26. 1. Herein, in the section dealing with that of one kind, the meaning should be understood as already stated.
vsm1.1:26.2:
2. In the section dealing with that of two kinds: fulfilling a training precept
announced by the Blessed One thus: “This should be done”
vsm1.1:26.4: not doing what is prohibited by him thus: “This should not be done” is avoiding.
vsm1.1:26.6: they keep (caranti) within that, they proceed as people who fulfil the virtues, thus it is keeping (cāritta);
vsm1.1:26.7: they preserve, they protect, they avoid, thus it is avoiding.
vsm1.1:26.8: Herein, keeping is accomplished by faith and energy; avoiding, by faith and mindfulness.
vsm1.1:26.9: This is how it is of two kinds as keeping and avoiding.
vsm1.1:27.1: 27. 3. In the second dyad good behaviour is the best kind of behaviour.
vsm1.1:27.2: Good behaviour itself is that of good behaviour;
vsm1.1:27.3: or what is announced for the sake of good behaviour is that of good behaviour.
vsm1.1:27.4: This is a term for virtue other than that which has livelihood as eighth.
vsm1.1:27.5: It is the initial stage of the life of purity consisting in the path, thus it is that of the beginning of the life of purity.
vsm1.1:27.6: This is a term for the virtue that has livelihood as eighth.
vsm1.1:27.7: It is the initial stage of the path because it has actually to be purified in the prior stage too.
vsm1.1:27.8: Hence it is said: “But his bodily action, his verbal action, and his livelihood have already been purified earlier” (M III 289).
vsm1.1:27.9: Or the training precepts called “lesser and minor” (D II 154) are that of good behaviour;
vsm1.1:27.10: the rest are that of the beginning of the life of purity.
vsm1.1:27.11: Or what is included in the Double Code (the bhikkhus' and bhikkhunīs' Pātimokkha) is that of the beginning of the life of purity;
vsm1.1:27.12: and that included in the duties set out in the Khandhakas of Vinaya is that of good behaviour.
vsm1.1:27.13: Through its perfection that of the beginning of the life of purity comes to be perfected.
vsm1.1:27.14:
Hence it is said also “that this bhikkhu shall fulfil the state consisting in the beginning of the life of purity
without having fulfilled the state consisting in good behaviour—that is not possible” (A III 14–15).
vsm1.1:27.15: So it is of two kinds as that of good behaviour and that of the beginning of the life of purity.
vsm1.1:28.1: 28. 4. In the third dyad virtue as abstinence is simply abstention from killing living things, etc.;
vsm1.1:28.2: the other kinds consisting in volition, etc., are virtue as non-abstinence.
vsm1.1:28.3: So it is of two kinds as abstinence and non-abstinence.
vsm1.1:29.1: 29. 5. In the fourth dyad there are two kinds of dependence: dependence through craving and dependence through false views.
vsm1.1:29.2:
Herein, that produced by one who wishes for a fortunate kind of becoming thus, “Through this virtuous
conduct rite I shall become a great deity or some minor deity” (M I 102),
vsm1.1:29.4: That produced through such false view about purification as “Purification is through virtuous conduct” (Vibh 374)
vsm1.1:29.6: But the supramundane, and the mundane that is the prerequisite for the aforesaid supramundane,
vsm1.1:29.8: So it is of two kinds as dependent and independent.
vsm1.1:30.1: 30. 6. In the fifth dyad temporary virtue is that undertaken after deciding on a time limit.
vsm1.1:30.2: Lifelong virtue is that practiced in the same way but undertaking it for as long as life lasts.
vsm1.1:30.3: So it is of two kinds as temporary and lifelong.
vsm1.1:31.1: 31. 7. In the sixth dyad the limited is that seen to be limited by gain, fame, relatives, limbs, or life.
vsm1.1:31.3:
And this is said in the Paṭisambhidā: “What is the virtue that has a limit? There is virtue
that has gain as its limit, there is virtue that has fame as its limit,
vsm1.1:31.4: there is virtue that has relatives as its limit, there is virtue that has limbs as its limit,
vsm1.1:31.5: there is virtue that has life as its limit.
vsm1.1:31.6:
What is virtue that has gain as its limit? Here someone with gain as cause, with gain
as condition, with gain as reason, transgresses a training precept as undertaken:
vsm1.1:31.7: that virtue has gain as its limit” (Paṭis I 43),
vsm1.1:31.8: and the rest should be elaborated in the same way.
vsm1.1:31.9:
Also in the answer dealing with the unlimited it is said: “What is virtue that does not have gain as its limit?
Here someone does not, with gain as cause, with gain as condition, with gain as reason,
even arouse the thought of transgressing a training precept as undertaken,
vsm1.1:31.10: how then shall he actually transgress it?
vsm1.1:31.11: That virtue does not have gain as its limit” (Paṭis I 44),
vsm1.1:31.12: and the rest should be elaborated in the same way.
vsm1.1:31.13: So it is of two kinds as limited and unlimited.
vsm1.1:32.1: 32. 8. In the seventh dyad all virtue subject to cankers is mundane;
vsm1.1:32.2: that not subject to cankers is supramundane.
vsm1.1:32.3: Herein, the mundane brings about improvement in future becoming and is a prerequisite for the escape from becoming,
vsm1.1:32.4:
according as it is said: “Discipline is for the purpose of restraint, restraint is for the purpose of non-remorse,
non-remorse is for the purpose of gladdening, gladdening is for the purpose of happiness,
vsm1.1:32.5:
happiness is for the purpose of tranquillity, tranquillity is for the purpose of bliss, bliss
is for the purpose of concentration, concentration is for the purpose of correct knowledge and vision,
vsm1.1:32.6:
correct knowledge and vision is for the purpose of dispassion, dispassion is for the purpose of fading
away of greed, fading away is for the purpose of deliverance,
vsm1.1:32.7:
deliverance is for the purpose of knowledge and vision of deliverance, knowledge and vision of deliverance
is for the purpose of complete extinction of craving, etc. through not clinging.
vsm1.1:32.8:
Talk has that purpose, counsel has that purpose, support has that purpose, giving ear has that purpose,
that is to say, the liberation of the mind through not clinging” (Vin V 164).
vsm1.1:32.9: The supramundane brings about the escape from becoming and is the plane of reviewing knowledge.
vsm1.1:32.10: So it is of two kinds as mundane and supramundane.
vsm1.1:33.1: 33. 9. In the first of the triads the inferior is produced by inferior zeal, purity of consciousness, energy, or inquiry;
vsm1.1:33.2: the medium is produced by medium zeal, etc.;
vsm1.1:33.3: the superior, by superior (zeal, and so on).
vsm1.1:33.4: That undertaken out of desire for fame is inferior;
vsm1.1:33.5: that undertaken out of desire for the fruits of merit is medium;
vsm1.1:33.6: that undertaken for the sake of the noble state thus, “This has to be done” is superior.
vsm1.1:33.7:
Or again, that defiled by self-praise and disparagement of others, etc., thus, “I am
possessed of virtue, but these other bhikkhus are ill-conducted and evil-natured” (M I 193), is inferior;
vsm1.1:33.10: Or again, that motivated by craving, the purpose of which is to enjoy continued existence, is inferior;
vsm1.1:33.11: that practiced for the purpose of one's own deliverance is medium;
vsm1.1:33.12: the virtue of the perfections practiced for the deliverance of all beings is superior.
vsm1.1:33.13: So it is of three kinds as inferior, medium, and superior.
vsm1.1:34.1:
34. 10. In the second triad that practiced out of self-regard by one who regards
self and desires to abandon what is unbecoming to self
vsm1.1:34.2: is virtue giving precedence to self.
vsm1.1:34.3: That practiced out of regard for the world and out of desire to ward off the censure of the world
vsm1.1:34.4: is virtue giving precedence to the world.
vsm1.1:34.5: That practiced out of regard for the Dhamma and out of desire to honour the majesty of the Dhamma
vsm1.1:34.6: is virtue giving precedence to the Dhamma.
vsm1.1:34.7: So it is of three kinds as giving precedence to self, and so on.
vsm1.1:35.1: 35. 11. In the third triad the virtue that in the dyads was called dependent (no. 5)
vsm1.1:35.2: is adhered-to because it is adhered-to through craving and false view.
vsm1.1:35.3: That practiced by the magnanimous ordinary man as the prerequisite of the path,
vsm1.1:35.4: and that associated with the path in trainers, are not-adhered-to.
vsm1.1:35.5: That associated with trainers' and non-trainers' fruition is tranquillized. So it is of three kinds as adhered-to, and so on.
vsm1.1:36.1: 36. 12. In the fourth triad that fulfilled by one who has committed no offence or has made amends after committing one is pure.
vsm1.1:36.2: So long as he has not made amends after committing an offence it is impure.
vsm1.1:36.3:
Virtue in one who is dubious about whether a thing constitutes an offence or about what
grade of offence has been committed or about whether he has committed an offence
vsm1.1:36.5: Herein, the meditator should purify impure virtue.
vsm1.1:36.6: If dubious, he should avoid cases about which he is doubtful and should get his doubts cleared up.
vsm1.1:36.7: In this way his mind will be kept at rest. So it is of three kinds as pure, and so on.
vsm1.1:37.1: 37. 13. In the fifth triad the virtue associated with the four paths and with the first three fruitions is that of the trainer.
vsm1.1:37.2: That associated with the fruition of Arahantship is that of the non-trainer.
vsm1.1:37.3: The remaining kinds are that of the neither-trainer-nor-non-trainer. So it is of three kinds as that of the trainer, and so on.
vsm1.1:38.1: 38. But in the world the nature of such and such beings is called their “habit” (sīla) of which they say:
vsm1.1:38.2:
“This one is of happy habit (sukha-sīla), this one is of unhappy habit,
this one is of quarrelsome habit, this one is of dandified habit.”
vsm1.1:38.3: Because of that it is said in the Paṭisambhidā figuratively: “Three kinds of virtue (habit):
vsm1.1:38.4: profitable virtue, unprofitable virtue, indeterminate virtue” (Paṭis I 44).
vsm1.1:38.5: So it is also called of three kinds as profitable, and so on.
vsm1.1:38.6:
Of these, the unprofitable is not included here since it has nothing whatever to do with the headings
beginning with the characteristic, which define virtue in the sense intended in this chapter.
vsm1.1:38.7: So the threefoldness should be understood only in the way already stated.
vsm1.1:39.1: 39. 14. In the first of the tetrads:
vsm1.1:39.2: The unvirtuous he cultivates, He visits not the virtuous, And in his ignorance he sees No fault in a transgression here,
vsm1.1:39.3: With wrong thoughts often in his mind His faculties he will not guard— Virtue in such a constitution Comes to partake of diminution.
vsm1.1:39.4:
But he whose mind is satisfied. With virtue that has been achieved, Who never
thinks to stir himself And take a meditation subject up,
vsm1.1:39.5: Contented with mere virtuousness, Nor striving for a higher state— His virtue bears the appellation Of that partaking of stagnation.
vsm1.1:39.6:
But who, possessed of virtue, strives With concentration for his aim— That bhikkhu's
virtue in its function Is called partaking of distinction.
vsm1.1:39.7:
Who finds mere virtue not enough But has dispassion for his goal— His virtue
through such aspiration Comes to partake of penetration.
vsm1.1:39.8: So it is of four kinds as partaking of diminution, and so on.
vsm1.1:40.1:
40. 15. In the second tetrad there are training precepts announced for bhikkhus to keep
irrespective of what is announced for bhikkhunīs.
vsm1.1:40.2: This is the virtue of bhikkhus.
vsm1.1:40.3: There are training precepts announced for bhikkhunīs to keep irrespective of what is announced for bhikkhus.
vsm1.1:40.4: This is the virtue of bhikkhunīs.
vsm1.1:40.5: The ten precepts of virtue for male and female novices are the virtue of the not fully admitted.
vsm1.1:40.6:
The five training precepts—ten when possible—as a permanent undertaking and eight as the factors of the Uposatha
Day, for male and female lay followers are the virtue of the laity.
vsm1.1:40.7: So it is of four kinds as the virtue of bhikkhus, and so on.
vsm1.1:41.1: 41. 16. In the third tetrad the non-transgression on the part of Uttarakuru human beings is natural virtue.
vsm1.1:41.2: Each clan's or locality's or sect's own rules of conduct are customary virtue.
vsm1.1:41.3:
The virtue of the Bodhisatta's mother described thus: “It is the necessary rule, Ānanda, that when the Bodhisatta has descended into
his mother's womb, no thought of men that is connected with the cords of sense desire comes to her” (D II 13), is necessary virtue.
vsm1.1:41.4:
But the virtue of such pure beings as Mahā Kassapa, etc., and of the Bodhisatta in his various
births is virtue due to previous causes.
vsm1.1:41.5: So it is of four kinds as natural virtue, and so on.
vsm1.1:42.1:
42. 17. In the fourth tetrad: (a) The virtue described by the Blessed One thus: “Here a bhikkhu dwells
restrained with the Pātimokkha restraint, possessed of the proper conduct and resort, and seeing
fear in the slightest fault, he trains himself by undertaking the precepts of training, (Vibh 244)”
vsm1.1:42.3:
(b) That described thus: “On seeing a visible object with the eye, he apprehends neither the signs nor the particulars through
which, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil and unprofitable states of covetousness and grief might invade him;
vsm1.1:42.4: he enters upon the way of its restraint, he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.
vsm1.1:42.5:
On hearing a sound with the ear … On smelling an odour with the nose … On tasting
a flavour with the tongue … On touching a tangible object with the body …
vsm1.1:42.6:
On cognizing a mental object with the mind, he apprehends neither the signs nor the particulars through which, if he left the mind
faculty unguarded, evil and unprofitable states of covetousness and grief might invade him; he enters upon the way of its restraint,
he guards the mind faculty, undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty (M I 180), is virtue of restraint of the sense faculties.
vsm1.1:42.7:
(c) Abstinence from such wrong livelihood as entails transgression of the six training precepts announced with respect to livelihood
and entails the evil states beginning with “Scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, pursuing gain with gain” (M II 75)
vsm1.1:42.9:
(d) Use of the four requisites that is purified by the reflection stated in the way beginning, “Reflecting wisely,
he uses the robe only for protection from cold” (M I 10) is called virtue concerning requisites.
